title: Episode 96: The Gaspee Affair: The First Blood of the American Revolution
description:
In June 1772, eighteen months before the Boston Tea Party, Rhode Island merchant John Brown and a band of Sons of Liberty attacked, boarded, shot the commander of, and burned to the waterline the despised British customs schooner HMS Gaspee in Narragansett Bay.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we sail into the choppy, fog-shrouded waters of Narragansett Bay, Rhode Island, to witness the forgotten first armed clash of the American Revolution: the burning of the Royal Navy customs schooner HMS Gaspee on June ninth, seventeen seventy-two. More than a year before Samuel Adams and the Sons of Liberty dumped British tea into Boston Harbor, Rhode Island merchants and sea captains took up muskets, rowed under cover of midnight darkness, shot a Royal Navy lieutenant in the groin, and blew his patrol ship out of the water. When an enraged King George the Third threatened to drag the conspirators to England in chains for trial, the crisis united the thirteen colonies through the Committees of Correspondence, lighting the fuse of revolution. Here is George with the full, explosive story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: RHODE ISLAND AND THE SMUGGLERS' PARADISE
To understand the explosive hostility that erupted in Narragansett Bay in seventeen seventy-two, one must understand the fiercely independent maritime culture of Rhode Island. Chartered by Roger Williams as a haven for religious freedom and civil liberty, Rhode Island possessed an extensive coastline of deep-water harbors, coves, and islands that made it the premier maritime trading hub of colonial America. Its economy was built almost entirely upon international commerce: importing molasses from the French and Dutch West Indies, distilling it into rum in Newport and Providence distilleries, and trading rum and manufactured goods across the Atlantic.
For generations, the British Crown had treated the colonies with 'salutary neglect,' allowing Rhode Island merchants to evade imperial customs duties with impunity. Bribery of royal customs collectors was common, and smuggling was viewed not as a criminal vice, but as a patriotic virtue that supported local employment. However, following the conclusion of the costly Seven Years' War in seventeen sixty-three, a debt-burdened British Parliament resolved to enforce the Navigation Acts and Townshend duties with ruthless military efficiency.
To police the defiant waters of Rhode Island, the British Admiralty dispatched the Royal Navy armed customs schooner HMS Gaspee, commanded by Lieutenant William Dudingston. Armed with eight carriage guns and a crew of thirty British sailors, the Gaspee was tasked with hunting down illicit colonial cargo. But Lieutenant Dudingston was not merely an officer executing his orders; he was an arrogant, haughty martinet who despised American colonials and treated every merchant captain with intolerable contempt. Merchants viewed British customs commissioners not as legitimate public servants, but as foreign extortionists preying on peaceful Rhode Island enterprise.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE TYRANT OF NARRAGANSETT BAY
Arriving in Narragansett Bay in March seventeen seventy-two, Lieutenant William Dudingston quickly inaugurated a virtual reign of terror on the coastal waters. Operating outside recognized naval protocols, Dudingston stopped, boarded, and searched every colonial vessel he encountered, regardless of whether they carried legal manifests. He seized small coastal market boats carrying firewood, vegetables, and livestock from local farmers, confiscating their goods without explanation and insulting prominent town magistrates who dared to question his authority.
Adding fuel to the fire, Dudingston ignored Rhode Island law by refusing to present his royal commission to Governor Joseph Wanton in Newport, boasting that Rhode Islanders were a lawless pack of pirates. When he seized the Rhode Island merchant sloop Fortune, loaded with twelve hogsheads of sugar and rum belonging to Nathanael Greene—the future Revolutionary War general—Dudingston refused to have the forfeiture adjudicated in Rhode Island's vice-admiralty court. Instead, he illegally shipped the vessel and its valuable cargo to Boston for condemnation, deeply offending Rhode Island's legal sovereignty.
Governor Wanton sent sharp official letters demanding that Dudingston produce his commission and cease harassing peaceful colonial commerce. Dudingston responded with open mockery, while his superior, Admiral John Montagu in Boston, threatened to hang anyone who interfered with the Gaspee as a traitor. In Providence, prominent merchant John Brown and sea captain Abraham Whipple held furious private conferences, agreeing that if Lieutenant Dudingston ever gave them an opening, Rhode Island would teach the Royal Navy an unforgettable lesson. Dudingston's abusive conduct alienated even staunch Tory loyalists, convincing the colony that imperial naval power was operating outside the rule of law.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE TRAP ON NAMQUID POINT
That fateful opening arrived on the morning of Tuesday, June ninth, seventeen seventy-two. Captain Benjamin Lindsey was commanding the packet sloop Hannah, sailing on its regular commercial run from Newport up Narragansett Bay toward Providence. Spotting the American merchant vessel, Lieutenant Dudingston signaled for the Hannah to heave-to and submit to a boarding search. Captain Lindsey, familiar with every shallow reef and sandbar in the bay, deliberately refused to stop, hoisting his colors and letting out his sails to outrun the British schooner.
Infuriated by Lindsey's defiance, Dudingston ordered the Gaspee into hot pursuit, firing warning shots across the Hannah's bow. For over twenty miles, the two vessels engaged in a high-speed chase up the bay. Knowing that the tide was falling and that the Gaspee had a deeper draft than his own shallow sloop, Lindsey steered the Hannah directly across the treacherous underwater sand spit extending off Namquid Point—now known as Gaspee Point—near Warwick.
Lindsey's lightweight sloop skimmed safely across the shallow sandbar with inches to spare. Minutes later, at shortly after three o'clock in the afternoon, the heavier Gaspee plowed at full sail directly into the hidden sandbar with a bone-jarring crash. The British schooner was hopelessly grounded, keeled over on its side in the wet mud. With the tide receding rapidly, Dudingston realized his ship was immobilized and could not be refloated until the next high tide at three o'clock the following morning. Captain Lindsey's tactical baiting of the British warship was hailed across Narragansett Bay as an audacious triumph of local seamanship.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE CALL TO ARMS AT SABIN TAVERN
Reaching the docks of Providence at five o'clock in the afternoon, Captain Lindsey immediately rushed to the counting house of John Brown, the wealthiest and most influential merchant in town. Lindsey reported the extraordinary news: the hated Gaspee was helpless, stranded hard aground on Namquid Point six miles south of the city, perfectly vulnerable to a night assault.
John Brown recognized that this was the moment Providence had been waiting for. He immediately dispatched a town crier through the streets with a drum, calling all interested citizens to assemble at James Sabin's tavern on South Main Street. By dusk, the tavern was packed to overflowing with prominent sea captains, merchants, young apprentices, and Sons of Liberty. In a back room around a roaring hearth, Brown and veteran privateer Captain Abraham Whipple organized the strike force.
Eight large, heavy wooden longboats—each equipped with five pairs of oars and capable of carrying a dozen men—were requisitioned from merchant wharves along the Providence River. Men melted lead over the tavern fire to cast musket balls, sharpened boarding cutlasses, and wrapped the iron oarlocks of the boats in sheepskin and greasy rags to ensure complete silence as they rowed through the midnight waters. Inside Sabin's tavern, men from every station of colonial society pledged mutual secrecy, knowing that discovery meant death on an English scaffold.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE MIDNIGHT ASSAULT ON THE MUDFLAT
At ten o'clock on the moonless night of June ninth, eight longboats carrying over sixty heavily armed Rhode Island patriots pushed silently away from Fenner's Wharf. Under the overall tactical command of Captain Abraham Whipple, the flotilla rowed down the ink-black waters of the Providence River in a single line, guided only by the rhythmic, muffled dipping of their oars.
Shortly after midnight, the dark, tilted silhouette of the stranded Gaspee loomed out of the fog near Namquid Point. At sixty yards, a British sentinel on the deck spotted the approaching boats and challenged: 'Who comes there?' Captain Whipple, standing in the bow of the lead boat, bellowed back: 'I am the sheriff of the County of Kent, God damn you, and I have come to arrest you!'
Lieutenant Dudingston rushed onto the deck in his nightshirt, brandishing a cutlass and shouting for the crew to man the swivel guns. But before the British sailors could fire, a young Rhode Islander in the bow named Joseph Bucklin raised his musket, turned to his companion, and said: 'Ephe, reach me your gun, and I will kill that man.' Bucklin fired. The lead ball tore through Dudingston's groin and abdomen, dropping the British lieutenant instantly to the deck in a pool of blood.
With a ferocious battle cry, the Rhode Islanders rammed their longboats against the Gaspee's wooden hull, swarming over the gunwales with cutlasses and boarding pikes. Surprised, outnumbered, and terrified by their commander's fall, the British crew surrendered after a brief, violent struggle without firing a single cannon. The swiftness and silence of the longboat assault completely paralyzed the Royal Navy crew, preventing them from discharging a single swivel gun.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE INFERNO OF THE GASPEE
Once in total command of the captured schooner, the Rhode Islanders demonstrated remarkable discipline. Captain Whipple ordered young Dr. John Mawney, who had joined the expedition with his medical instruments, to tend to the wounded British lieutenant. In the ship's cabin, Mawney dressed Dudingston's severe groin wound and stanched the bleeding, saving the royal officer's life.
Whipple ordered the captured British crew and their wounded lieutenant loaded into the longboats along with their personal clothing and sea chests. They were rowed safely ashore and landed at Pawtuxet Village, where Dudingston was placed in the care of a local family. Meanwhile, back on the grounded schooner, Brown and Whipple's men systematically searched the vessel for royal customs manifests and official documents, confiscating all papers.
They then smashed open casks of rum and pitch, soaking the cabin, decks, and rigging. Fire was set to the forward hold. As the eight longboats rowed back into the dark bay toward Providence, flames engulfed the wooden schooner from bow to stern, lighting the midnight sky for miles around. At dawn, the fire reached the Gaspee's powder magazine: a colossal explosion tore the ship apart, sending shattered timber and iron cannons into the sky and burning the despised vessel down to the waterline. The fiery destruction of the Gaspee illuminated the shores of Warwick and Providence, signaling the end of passive colonial submission.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE ROYAL COMMISSION AND THE SEEDS OF REVOLUTION
When news of the violent destruction of a Royal Navy warship reached London, King George the Third and his ministers were incensed. The Crown issued an extraordinary royal proclamation offering a massive reward of one thousand pounds for the apprehension of the ringleaders and created a special Royal Commission of Inquiry composed of imperial admiralty judges and colonial governors.
Most alarmingly, the Crown decreed that any person indicted in the burning of the Gaspee would be stripped of their constitutional right to a local jury trial, placed in irons, and transported across the Atlantic to England to face trial for high treason—a crime punishable by drawing and quartering. Yet despite the fact that hundreds of Providence residents knew precisely who had planned and executed the attack, not a single Rhode Islander ever broke silence. For six months, the Royal Commission interrogated local merchants and fishermen, but encountered a wall of absolute, impenetrable collective amnesia. Not a single person was ever prosecuted.
The threat to transport American colonists to England for treason galvanized patriotic outrage across all thirteen colonies. In Virginia, young burgesses Thomas Jefferson, Patrick Henry, and Richard Henry Lee were so alarmed by the royal commission that they established the permanent inter-colonial Committees of Correspondence, creating the vital communications network that coordinated the continental resistance.
The burning of the Gaspee on June tenth, seventeen seventy-two was not a mere riot; it was the crossing of the Rubicon, the first organized armed attack against the armed forces of the British Empire. Today, Rhode Island proudly celebrates 'Gaspee Day' every June with parades and commemorative bonfires, honoring the bold sea dogs who dared to shed the first blood of American liberty. Rhode Island's armed defiance inspired patriots throughout the colonies, proving that ordinary citizens could strike back against imperial tyranny.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The burning of the Gaspee proved that American colonists were willing to meet royal tyranny with armed resistance, lighting the fuse of revolution eighteen months before Boston. I'm Rebecca. Join us next week as we enter the glittering summer palaces of Gilded Age Newport.
